prompt: Executives want a five-sentence version of each 40-page report.
trap: Capping tokens would just cut the report off.

prompt: After each support call, the agent wants an automatic recap of the issue and the resolution from the transcript.
tells: recap of the issue and the resolution
why: Conversation summarization pulls issue and resolution from a transcript.
trap: The input is already a transcript, so this is text summarization.

prompt: A legal team wants a summary made only of the most important original sentences, unchanged.
why: Extractive summarization picks original sentences; abstractive rewrites.
trap: Key phrases are fragments, not full sentences.

prompt: A busy channel has 300 messages since yesterday. Give each person a short digest.
trap: Listing topics isn't the same as telling what happened.

prompt: A manager returns from vacation to a 60-email thread and wants the key decisions in a paragraph.
why: A paragraph of key points is summarization.
trap: Key phrases would give fragments, not decisions.

prompt: A product team wants a short, newly worded recap of each support conversation, not copied sentences.
why: Abstractive summarization writes a new, shorter version.

prompt: Lawyers want a short brief of each new court ruling, written in plain words.
tells: short brief of each new court ruling
why: A short version of long text is summarization.
trap: Extracting fields doesn't give a brief.

prompt: When a bot hands a chat to a human agent, the agent sees three lines covering the problem and what's been tried.
tells: three lines covering the problem and what's been tried
why: Conversation summarization condenses the chat for the handoff.
trap: The history exists already; the agent needs it condensed.
